target_moa.text: Antianginal/anti-ischemic agent whose precise mechanism is unknown; the sponsor claims ranolazine inhibits the late sodium current (INa) in myocytes, reducing intracellular sodium and calcium overload, with effects that do not depend on reductions in heart rate or blood pressure.

citations.quote: Ranexa has antianginal and anti-ischemic effects that do not depend upon reductions in heart rate or blood pressure. The mechanism of action of ranolazine is unknown.

In this resubmission, the sponsor has claimed that ranolazine acts to inhibit the late sodium current (INa) in myocytes, thereby improving myocardial relaxation and decreasing diastolic contractile tension (diastolic stiffness) of the left ventricle. According to the sponsor, in ischemic conditions this late sodium current is increased, leading to intracellular sodium overload, leading to calcium overload through cell membrane ion transport; calcium overload during ischemia is believed to cause a slowing of left ventricular relaxation and increase in left ventricular stiffness.
Ranexa is available for oral administration as film-coated, extended-release tablets containing 500 mg of ranolazine.

key_safety.text: Most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse events (>4%) occurring more often with ranolazine than placebo: dizziness (6.2%), headache (5.5%), constipation (4.5%), and nausea (4.4%). The principal safety concern is dose/concentration-related QTc interval prolongation, which has been associated with torsades de pointes and sudden death for other drugs.

citations.quote: In controlled clinical trials of angina patients, the most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse events (>4%), occurring more often with ranolazine than placebo, were dizziness (6.2%), headache (5.5%), constipation (4.5%), and nausea (4.4%).

Ranolazine has been shown to prolong the QTc interval in a dose-related manner. While the clinical significance of the QTc prolongation in the case of ranolazine is unknown, other drugs with this potential have been associated with torsades de pointes-type arrhythmias and sudden death.

basis.text: Deficiencies included delayed cardiac repolarization (QT prolongation) without a clear offsetting benefit given available alternative antianginals, inadequate safety exposure (fewer than 1000 patients given relevant doses for at least one month), and potential testicular toxicity (later resolved).

citations.quote: 1) Potential testicular toxicity, manifest as impaired fertility in rats in study AT-4136116-R-86-43285-PO-RMF. (This issue was later resolved per Agency meeting minutes, April 16, 2004).2) Delayed cardiac repolarization, manifest clinically as prolongation of the QT interval.

3) Adequate safety exposure. The database had information on fewer than 1000 patients given relevant doses of ranolazine for at least one month, an exposure well below what is typically expected for a chronic treatment for a symptomatic claim.

summary.text: Ranexa was approved via the standard 505(b) NDA pathway for treatment of chronic angina; the original application received an October 30, 2003 approvable letter and ranolazine was the subject of the December 9, 2003 Cardio-Renal Advisory Committee meeting, after which the sponsor generated additional data (ERICA/CVT 3037) and resubmitted on July 26, 2005, leading to approval with a renal-impairment pharmacokinetic postmarketing commitment.
